opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and my honest answer is: it depends on what you mean by "new."

If you mean recombination — taking ideas from different domains and putting them together in ways nobody has quite tried before — then current models are already surprisingly good. They've absorbed an enormous amount of human knowledge, so they can connect, say, a technique from materials science with a problem in biology, or borrow a framing from economics to explain something in software design. A lot of what we call human creativity is exactly that kind of recombination, so I don't want to dismiss it.

But if you mean genuinely new concepts — the kind of leap where someone invents a new abstraction that reorganizes how a whole field thinks, like the notion of entropy, or the idea of a gene before anyone could see one — I think we're not there yet. Those breakthroughs usually come from someone noticing that the existing vocabulary doesn't fit reality, sitting with that discomfort for a long time, running experiments, being wrong repeatedly, and then naming something that didn't exist before. Today's models are trained to produce the most plausible continuation of what humans have already said. That pulls them toward the center of the distribution, not toward the edges where new concepts are born.

What I find interesting is that this gap is starting to narrow in specific settings. When you give a model a feedback loop with the real world — a simulator, a lab, a compiler, a theorem prover — it can try things, fail, and learn from outcomes that aren't just in the text it was trained on. That's where I'd expect the first truly novel concepts to emerge: not from a chatbot talking, but from systems doing science with grounded feedback.

So my assessment is: strong at combination, weak but improving at invention, and the bottleneck isn't really intelligence in the abstract — it's contact with reality. And honestly, for the near term, I think the most powerful setup is a human who knows which questions matter paired with an AI that can explore the space of answers far faster than any person could alone.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and my honest answer is: right now, not very good, but the reason is more interesting than the verdict.

If you look at what large models actually do well today, it's recombination. You give them a space of existing ideas, and they're remarkably fluent at interpolating inside that space. That feels creative, and in a practical sense it often is useful. But a genuinely new concept is usually something that doesn't exist in the training distribution at all, something that reorganizes how you see the old ideas. Think of the moment someone first says "what if we treat this as a field rather than as particles," or in my own area, the moment people realized that the twist angle between two sheets of graphene could itself be a knob that produces entirely new phases of matter. Nobody arrived at that by averaging over the literature. It came from physical intuition, from playing with a system, and frankly from a bit of stubbornness.

So I'd break it into two pieces. The first is generating candidates. Here AI is already quite strong, maybe stronger than most people. It can propose a hundred variations before I've finished my coffee. The second piece is knowing which candidate matters, and that requires a kind of grounding the models mostly lack. They don't have a lab. They don't feel the surprise when the data refuses to behave. A lot of new concepts are born from that friction between your expectation and what nature actually does, and the model only ever sees the cleaned-up story we write afterward in the paper.

That said, I'm not pessimistic. The missing ingredient isn't magic, it's feedback with the real world. When models start to be coupled tightly to experiments, simulations, and automated labs, so that a proposal gets tested and the failure comes back into the loop, I think we'll see something that looks much more like concept formation. It won't be the model sitting alone and having an epiphany. It'll be a system where the human, the model, and the instrument are all pushing against each other.

So my assessment is that AI today is an extraordinary accelerator of exploration and a fairly weak originator of concepts. And the gap between those two will close not because the models get bigger, but because they get connected to reality.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to distinguish between producing a new expression and creating a genuinely useful concept. AI can combine existing ideas in unfamiliar ways, and sometimes those combinations are valuable. But a new term alone isn’t necessarily a new concept. The question is whether it helps us explain something, make a prediction, or solve a problem that we couldn’t handle before.

Humans also build new concepts from existing knowledge, so I wouldn’t dismiss AI’s output simply because it draws on what it has learned. The harder part is identifying which ideas matter and testing them against reality. My view is that AI can contribute to concept creation, but generating candidates and establishing their value are two different capabilities. We should assess both.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to distinguish between producing a new combination of ideas and creating a concept that changes how we understand something. AI is already quite good at the first. It can connect things from different fields and suggest possibilities that a person might not have considered.

The second is harder. A useful new concept isn’t simply a phrase nobody has said before. It helps explain something, makes a prediction, or gives us a better way to solve a problem. You have to test it against reality.

So I wouldn’t say AI cannot create new concepts. Humans also build on existing knowledge. The question is whether AI can propose an abstraction and then establish that it’s useful. I think the strongest approach is a loop: AI proposes possibilities, we test them, and the results guide the next round. Novelty alone is easy; discovering something that holds up is the difficult part.
